newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: E.Asian Grain - Buyers sidelined, except for Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: E.Asian Grain - Buyers sidelined, except for Taiwan.

text.p: Holidays in Japan and South Korea, along with high corn premiums, may sideline grains and oilseeds buyers this week despite a fall in trans-Pacific freight rates and lower prices in Chicago, grain traders said on Monday.

The only action would be tenders in Taiwan for at least 72,000 tonnes of corn and 12,000 tonnes of soybeans from the United States, the traders said. Wheat buyers from the Philippines will also probably sit it out this week.
"It should be a quiet market because of Chusok, the Korean Thanksgiving holiday. No one can enter the market at all," a Seoul-based Japanese trader said. "The market is already in a holiday mood."
Some traders in Seoul said buyers might buy several cargoes of corn for June to July shipment if prices in the United States dipped further over the next few days.
A trader with Cheiljedang Corp in South Korea said he expected wheat prices to see a short-term rally as worries spread of frost hitting Canada's wheat crop.

In Japan, importers had covered more than 60 percent of their January/March requirement for U.S. corn, and premiums for U.S. corn were currently quoted at around 99 cents a bushel on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) March contract, traders said.
"Local feed makers are hesitating to buy if more than 100 cents of premiums are offered," a corn trader at a major trade house said. "I don't expect active buying from Japan until early October."
Japanese importers have also purchased more than 30 percent of their U.S. soybean needs for November shipment.
Delayed talks between crushers and feed makers over local soymeal prices for October/December 1996 deliveries would make importers hesitant, traders said.
Nearby freight rates on the U.S. Gulf/Japan route have fallen to below $19 a tonne at one stage last week, shipping industry officials said.
Freight rates fell from about $23 in June and $38 in May, mainly because newly-built Panamax-sized ships were entering the market, the officials said.
Taiwan traders said there may be two tenders this week.
The state-owned Taiwan Sugar Corp was expected to tender for a combined shipment of 18,000 tonnes of No.2 U.S. corn and 12,000 tonnes of No.2 U.S. soybeans, traders said.
The shipment is slated for delivery from the U.S. Gulf of Mexico from October 25 to November 10.
Traders said Taiwan's FGEP group is also in the market for a 54,000-tonne corn shipment to be delivered in December.
The FGEP group is made up of Fwu Sow Grain, Great Wall Enterprise, President Enterprise and Ever Smile Feed Mill Co.
Taiwanese buyers said pressures from the imminent U.S. corn harvest and the lack of strong weather concerns could keep prices low.

"Corn will remain bearish for nearby harvest season as long as no serious frost comes into play," an executive at Taiwan's Formosa Oilseed said. Formosa Oilseed is a key buyer in Taiwan's Members Feed Industry Group.
